summary.text: The Rule 167 zero patterns are matched, using Pascal’s identity modulo 2, with an odd-binomial-coefficient invariant; specializing at the center and applying binary parity reductions shows that the center bit is zero exactly at powers of two. Since \(n\mid 2^{n+1}\) holds exactly when \(n\) is a power of two, the floor indicator equals the complement of the new center bit, and appending that bit to the binary prefix gives the recurrence.

full_proof.text:
Let \(C(t,x)\in\{0,1\}\) denote the state at time \(t\geq 0\) and position \(x\in\mathbb Z\) of the Rule 167 cellular automaton begun from one black cell at the origin. Thus
\[
 C(0,x)=\begin{cases}1,&x=0,\\0,&x\ne0,\end{cases}
\]
and \(C(t+1,x)\) is obtained by applying Rule 167 to
\((C(t,x-1),C(t,x),C(t,x+1))\).

Number the eight neighborhoods by the integer \(4L+2C+R\), where \(L,C,R\in\{0,1\}\). Rule 167 outputs the corresponding bit of \(167\). Since
\[
167=2^7+2^5+2^2+2^1+2^0,
\]
its output is zero precisely for neighborhood indices \(3,4,6\). Equivalently,
\[
\operatorname{Rule}_{167}(L,C,R)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(L,C,R)\in\{(0,1,1),(1,0,0),(1,1,0)\}.             \tag{1}
\]
The output is always either zero or one.

We first prove a description of all zero cells in the spacetime diagram. For \(t\geq1\) and \(x\in\mathbb Z\), define the assertion \(P(t,x)\) as follows. It is false unless \(x+t\) is even. When \(x+t\) is even, put
\[
 j=\frac{x+t-2}{2}.
\]
Then \(P(t,x)\) means
\[
0\leq j<t
\quad\text{and}\quad
\binom{t-1}{j}\equiv1\pmod2.                         \tag{2}
\]
We claim that
\[
 C(t,x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P(t,x)          \tag{3}
\]
for every \(t\geq1\) and every integer \(x\).

We prove (3) by induction on \(t\). At time \(1\), direct examination of the initial configuration shows that the only zero output is at \(x=1\). Indeed, the neighborhoods at \(x=-1,0,1\) are respectively \(001,010,100\), and away from these positions the neighborhood is \(000\). Rule 167 outputs one on \(000,001,010\) and zero on \(100\). On the other hand, for \(t=1\), condition (2) forces
\[
 j=\frac{x-1}{2}=0,
\]
so it also holds precisely when \(x=1\), because \(\binom00=1\). Thus the claim holds at time \(1\).

For the induction step, it is useful first to derive the recurrence obeyed by \(P\). We claim that, for \(t\geq1\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(t+1,x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad{}
&\bigl(P(t,x-1)\land\neg P(t,x)\land\neg P(t,x+1)\bigr)\\
&\lor\bigl(\neg P(t,x-1)\land P(t,x)\land P(t,x+1)\bigr)\\
&\lor\bigl(\neg P(t,x-1)\land\neg P(t,x)\land P(t,x+1)\bigr).
                                                               \tag{4}
\end{aligned}
\]
Here is the verification. If \(x+t+1\) is odd, then \(P(t+1,x)\) is false. In this parity case, \(x+t\) is even, while \(x-1+t\) and \(x+1+t\) are odd. Thus both \(P(t,x-1)\) and \(P(t,x+1)\) are false, irrespective of the middle assertion, and every disjunct on the right of (4) is false.

Now suppose \(x+t+1\) is even and set
\[
 j=\frac{x+t-1}{2}.
\]
The parity condition for \(P(t,x)\) fails, while the parity conditions for the two neighboring assertions hold. After taking account of their range conditions, the relevant binomial coefficients are
\[
P(t,x-1):\ \binom{t-1}{j-1},
\qquad
P(t,x+1):\ \binom{t-1}{j},
\]
and the coefficient for \(P(t+1,x)\) is \(\binom tj\). Pascal’s identity gives
\[
\binom tj=\binom{t-1}{j-1}+\binom{t-1}{j}.             \tag{5}
\]
Modulo \(2\), the sum on the right is odd exactly when precisely one of its two summands is odd. The range requirements at \(j=0\) and \(j=t\) say the same thing if coefficients outside their natural range are regarded as zero. Since the middle assertion is false in this parity case, the first and third disjuncts of (4) express exactly this exclusive alternative. This proves (4).

Assume now that (3) holds at time \(t\). A state is one exactly when it is not zero, since all states belong to \(\{0,1\}\). Therefore, after replacing each zero state by \(P\) and each one state by \(\neg P\), the three zero-producing neighborhoods in (1) become exactly the three disjuncts on the right of (4). Consequently Rule 167 produces zero at \((t+1,x)\) exactly when \(P(t+1,x)\) holds. This completes the induction and proves (3).

We now specialize this characterization to the central column. The necessary binomial parity fact is
\[
 \binom{2m-1}{m-1}\equiv1\pmod2
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 m\text{ is a power of }2                              \tag{6}
\]
for every \(m\geq1\).

We prove (6) by strong induction on \(m\). We use the following two elementary parity identities:
\[
\binom{2A+1}{2B+1}\equiv\binom AB\pmod2,
\qquad
\binom{2A+1}{2B}\equiv\binom AB\pmod2.                 \tag{7}
\]
They follow, for example, by working with polynomials modulo \(2\):
\[
(1+X)^{2A+1}=(1+X)\bigl((1+X)^2\bigr)^A
\equiv(1+X)(1+X^2)^A\pmod2.
\]
Comparing the coefficients of \(X^{2B+1}\) and \(X^{2B}\) gives (7).

The assertion (6) is immediate for \(m=1\). Suppose first that \(m=2q\) is even. Then, by the first identity in (7),
\[
\binom{2m-1}{m-1}
 =\binom{4q-1}{2q-1}
 \equiv \binom{2q-1}{q-1}\pmod2.                       \tag{8}
\]
By the induction hypothesis, the last coefficient is odd exactly when \(q\) is a power of two. This is equivalent to \(m=2q\) being a power of two.

Suppose instead that \(m>1\) is odd, say \(m=2q+1\), where \(q\geq1\). The second identity in (7) gives
\[
\binom{2m-1}{m-1}
 =\binom{4q+1}{2q}
 \equiv\binom{2q}{q}\pmod2.                            \tag{9}
\]
The central binomial coefficient \(\binom{2q}{q}\) is even for \(q\geq1\). Indeed, the standard adjacent-binomial identity yields
\[
\binom{2q}{q}=2\binom{2q-1}{q-1}.
\]
Thus the coefficient in (9) is even. At the same time an odd integer greater than one cannot be a power of two. Hence both sides of (6) are false in this case. This proves (6).

We can now determine the middle-column bit. Let \(n\geq2\). At \(x=0\), the parity prerequisite in \(P(n,0)\) is that \(n\) be even. If \(n\) is odd, then \(P(n,0)\) is false; also, since \(n>1\), \(n\) is not a power of two.

If \(n\) is even, write \(n=2m\), with \(m\geq1\). Then
\[
 j=\frac{n-2}{2}=m-1,
\]
and the bounds \(0\leq j<n\) automatically hold. Therefore
\[
P(n,0)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\binom{2m-1}{m-1}\text{ is odd}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
m\text{ is a power of two},                            \tag{10}
\]
where the final equivalence is (6). Since \(n=2m\), this is equivalent to \(n\) being a power of two. Combining the even and odd cases with (3), we obtain the crucial central-column characterization
\[
 C(n,0)=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 n=2^k\text{ for some }k\geq0                         \tag{11}
\]
for every \(n\geq2\). Because \(C(n,0)\) is a bit, it follows also that
\[
 C(n,0)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&n\text{ is a power of }2,\\
 1,&n\text{ is not a power of }2.
 \end{cases}                                           \tag{12}
\]

Next consider the floor term in the proposed recurrence. Put
\[
 r=2^{n+1}\bmod n.
\]
Since \(r\) is a nonnegative integer,
\[
\left\lfloor(1/2)^r\right\rfloor
=
\begin{cases}
1,&r=0,\\
0,&r>0.
\end{cases}                                            \tag{13}
\]
For \(n>0\), the condition \(r=0\) is equivalent to
\[
 n\mid 2^{n+1}.                                        \tag{14}
\]
Every positive divisor of a power of the prime \(2\) is itself a power of \(2\): repeatedly removing factors of \(2\), any remaining factor would be an odd divisor greater than one of a power of \(2\), which is impossible. Thus (14) implies \(n=2^k\) for some \(k\).

Conversely, suppose \(n=2^k\). To see that \(2^k\mid2^{n+1}\), it suffices that \(k\leq n+1=2^k+1\). The elementary inequality \(k\leq2^k\) holds for every \(k\geq0\), by induction: it is clear for \(k=0\), and from \(k\leq2^k\) and \(2^k\geq1\) one gets \(k+1\leq2^{k+1}\). Hence the required divisibility holds. We have therefore shown, for \(n\geq2\),
\[
\left\lfloor(1/2)^{(2^{n+1}\bmod n)}\right\rfloor
=
\begin{cases}
1,&n\text{ is a power of }2,\\
0,&n\text{ is not a power of }2.
\end{cases}                                            \tag{15}
\]
Comparing (12) and (15), we conclude that
\[
 C(n,0)=1-
 \left\lfloor(1/2)^{(2^{n+1}\bmod n)}\right\rfloor.   \tag{16}
\]

Finally, by definition, \(a(n)\) is the integer represented by the first \(n+1\) middle-column bits:
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}C(k,0)2^{n-k}.                     \tag{17}
\]
For \(n\geq1\), split off the final summand and factor \(2\) from all preceding terms:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)
&=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}C(k,0)2^{n-k}+C(n,0)\\
&=2\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}C(k,0)2^{(n-1)-k}+C(n,0)\\
&=2a(n-1)+C(n,0).                                      \tag{18}
\end{aligned}
\]
This is simply the usual operation of appending the bit \(C(n,0)\) to a binary numeral.

Substituting (16) into (18) gives, for every integer \(n\geq2\),
\[
\boxed{
 a(n)=2a(n-1)+1-
 \left\lfloor(1/2)^{(2^{n+1}\bmod n)}\right\rfloor
 }.
\]
This is the claimed recurrence.
